I've been farming here in Quzhou County for over thirty years. My family has 6 mu of good flat land, and I've always followed the wheat-maize rotation — it's the safest and most reliable system here on the North China Plain. The winter wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage, and now in April it's coming up green and strong. I'll finish managing it through to harvest in early June, then immediately plant summer maize using no-tillage — there's no time to waste between crops, and the soil holds moisture better that way.

For the wheat, I use improved varieties like Jimai 22 that I buy from the seed station. I trust them because they yield steady and resist lodging. I've already given it winter irrigation and one spring topdressing. Now I'll irrigate two more times — once at jointing and once at grain filling — and spray for aphids and rust. I apply about 25 kg of nitrogen per mu in total, split between basal compound fertilizer and topdressing urea, plus some phosphorus and potassium from the compound bag. I don't bother with much potassium alone — the compound fertilizer has enough.

For the maize, I'll plant Denghai 605 hybrid seed — everyone in the village grows it because it gives 1,100 jin per mu or more if the weather cooperates. No ploughing; I just sow directly into the wheat stubble right after harvest. Two irrigations will be enough for maize — one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling — and I'll spray herbicide once and insecticide twice. I use less fertilizer on maize than wheat, about 20 kg nitrogen per mu, again mostly from compound fertilizer plus a urea topdressing.

I don't gamble with new crops. Cotton prices have been unpredictable, and vegetables need too much labor and market access. Wheat and maize give me food security and cash income I can count on.
